title: From synthetic enterprise data evaluations to real Microsoft Copilot AI confidence
abstract: At a glance Evaluating Microsoft Copilot at enterprise scale requires test data that captures the full complexity of real organizations, yet real enterprise data contains sensitive information that cannot be used for evaluation under any circumstances. To resolve this tension, we built Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform: full-scale synthetic enterprise environments grounded in publicly available real-world data sources such as O*NET occupational data, online job postings, and SEC filings. The synthetic environments mimic real business workflows, helping Microsoft find issues that generic benchmarks would miss. Safety and privacy are built into the platform by design. Every environment is fully synthetic and automated content-safety checks keep the generated data free of harmful or personally identifiable material. Every day, millions of knowledge workers around the world rely on Microsoft Copilot to draft documents, summarize meetings, surface relevant information, and accelerate productivity. Behind the scenes, this is powered by a network of AI systems, and ensuring they work as intended requires a thoughtful approach to evaluation. At Microsoft, we know that high performance doesn’t come from guesswork. It comes from testing, measuring, and iterating constantly. Healthcare organizations are constantly synthesizing safety signals from across teams so that they can make faster, better decisions that directly influence patient outcomes and regulatory confidence. They may ask Copilot to summarize a meeting and extract action items for their teams. Within seconds, Copilot delivers a structured summary citing specific discussion points from the transcript. But how do we ensure this response is accurate, complete, and properly grounded in the meeting content? This is where our evaluation system comes in. We’ve developed a structured evaluation strategy called Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform , which includes industry specific evaluation datasets designed to test AI systems against realistic enterprise scenarios, grounded in three core pillars: Synthetic enterprise environments : simulated Microsoft Copilot environments with realistic users, meetings, emails, documents, and organizational structures that replicate the complexity of real organizations without using any customer data Automated query generation pipelines for rapid, reproducible creation of evaluation datasets Structured quality frameworks to ensure synthetic data meets the bar for meaningful evaluation Figure 1: Components of Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform Together, these pillars help us answer two fundamental questions: Is Microsoft Copilot actually doing what our users need it to do, and can we prove it without ever touching their data ? In this blog post, we’ll walk through our evaluation system and processes, from synthetic environment generation to automated query pipelines, and how it all comes together to establish the first standardized evaluation baseline for Microsoft Copilot. Synthetic enterprise environments Evaluating enterprise AI requires test data that captures the full complexity of real organizations: reporting structures, project histories, communication patterns, and domain specific workflows. But real enterprise data contains sensitive information that cannot be used for evaluation under any circumstances. This is the central tension we set out to resolve. Rather than relying on small, manually curated test fixtures, we generate full scale synthetic environments : simulated enterprise workspaces, each with realistic organizational structures, communication histories, and work artifacts. In Microsoft terminology, each of these simulated workspaces is called a “tenant”. A tenant is an isolated organizational environment with its own users, data, and configurations. title: Managing Amazon Bedrock costs end to end: A playbook for FinOps and platform teams
abstract: Cost management for generative AI is a shared responsibility between the teams that build applications and the teams accountable for cloud spend. Many teams start by comparing per-model token rates and asking application teams to shorten prompts. Those steps help, but they don’t answer the questions that finance and engineering leaders ask as usage scales: which team spent this, on which workload, and was that spend inside an approved budget? Agentic workloads make those questions more pressing. A conversational assistant typically issues one model invocation per user turn. An agentic workflow, such as an AI coding assistant that plans a change, reads files, calls tools, and iterates, issues many invocations per task and carries a larger context on each one. Token consumption therefore scales with the degree of autonomy you grant the workflow and the size of the context it carries, rather than with the number of user interactions. Because consumption is a function of how a workload is designed and operated, cost management for generative AI is an architectural and operational discipline. Published averages are a poor substitute for your own numbers: use the AWS Pricing Calculator and the Amazon Bedrock pricing page to model rates, and use Step 2 of this post to measure what your workloads actually consume. The fix isn’t a cheaper model or a smaller prompt. It’s an operating model: a repeatable loop that attributes every dollar to an owner, makes every request observable, alerts on and enforces budgets before overspend compounds, optimizes the platform defaults that drive most waste, and reviews the whole system on a cadence. In this post, you learn how to manage Amazon Bedrock cost in five steps. You attribute every dollar to an owner, make every request observable, control spend with budgets and enforcement, optimize the platform defaults that drive most avoidable spend, and operate a review cadence that turns data into decisions. This approach is built from AWS building blocks, and you can customize it and apply it to your own environment. The post is written for two audiences: FinOps practitioners who own attribution, chargeback, budgets, and anomaly review, and platform engineering teams who own logging, request metadata, enforcement, and routing defaults. The operating model in one view Five stages, run as a loop. Attribute: every Amazon Bedrock dollar lands on an identity, team, and application in the billing pipeline. Observe: every request is logged with enough metadata to explain what generated the spend. Enforce: budgets have teeth, with alerts at minimum and hard blocks where the risk demands them. Optimize: the platform defaults (model routing, caching, token limits) remove waste centrally instead of asking every team to be careful. Operate: a small scorecard and a review cadence turn the data into decisions. FinOps leads stages one and five. Platform engineering leads two through four. The review is joint. The stages are sequenced deliberately. Each one depends on the ones before it, and teams that jump straight to optimization without attribution and observability are guessing. Figure 1: The five-stage operating model, run as a continuous loop Stage 1: Attribute every dollar You can’t manage what you can’t attribute, and everything downstream (chargeback, budgets, enforcement, anomaly detection) depends on this stage. The foundation is the granular cost attribution of Amazon Bedrock (see Introducing granular cost attribution for Amazon Bedrock ): Amazon Bedrock automatically attributes inference costs to the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) principal that made the call, across all models, with no resources to manage. The caller’s ARN lands in the line_item_iam_principal column of the AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR) 2.0 , and coverage spans IAM users, roles, federated identities, and API keys. title: Preview web apps live as your coding agent builds them with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime
abstract: Coding agents now build working web apps: a dashboard, a product page, a prototype that a product team wants to try. The fastest way to review that work is to open the app, use it, ask for a change, and check the result. That loop works well when the app keeps running where the agent edits it, so each change shows up in the browser within seconds. When the app must be copied out and deployed somewhere else first, every change waits for a deployment, and the review slows down to that pace. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with your choice of agent framework and foundation model (FM). AgentCore runtime , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, runs each agent session in its own isolated microVM. With Session endpoints , you can open an app running in that session from your own browser. Session Endpoints give each session an authenticated URL that forwards each request’s HTTP method, path, query string, and body, and WebSocket connections, to the ports you allow. You can watch the page update as the agent saves each file. In this post, you deploy a coding agent that keeps a Vite website running in its session, then open one local page with a chat on the left and the live website on the right. You ask the agent to switch the site to a dark color theme, follow its steps as they stream in, and watch the website change without a refresh. Finally, you look at what happens internally: a second port in the same session, and the requests the Session endpoint refuses. The complete sample, including the notebook this post follows, is in the 14-remote-access folder of the agentcore-samples GitHub repo . How Session endpoints work Each session gets its own Session endpoint, and six details shape how you use it. You choose which ports it reaches. You set allowedPorts when you call CreateAgentRuntime : 1–5 entries, each a single port or a range within 8000–12000, excluding the reserved platform ports . Allowing a port doesn’t start a server, so your application must listen on it, bound to 0.0.0.0 . The URL arrives with the session. The InvokeAgentRuntime response carries it in the X-Amzn-Bedrock-AgentCore-Runtime-Session-Endpoint-Url header, which SDKs that model it expose as sessionEndpointUrl . Every request is authenticated. For a runtime that uses AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) , each HTTP request, HTTP/2 stream, and WebSocket handshake carries a Signature Version 4 (SigV4) signature. The caller also needs bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntimeProxy on the runtime and its runtime endpoint. For a runtime with an inbound JSON Web Token (JWT) authorizer , each request carries a bearer token instead. Knowing the URL doesn’t grant access. The host name selects the port. Your client connects on port 443 regardless of the target port, and a prefix on the host name chooses the port inside the session: https://8090--<session-endpoint-id>.runtime.bedrock-agentcore.<region>.on.aws/index.html https://8081--<session-endpoint-id>.runtime.bedrock-agentcore.<region>.on.aws/status It carries the protocols your server speaks. HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 requests, including server-sent events and gRPC, and WebSocket connections all pass through. This walkthrough uses HTTP/1.1 and WebSocket. It’s scoped to one session. The URL needs credentials on every request and lasts only as long as the session, so use it to build, test, and review what your agent produces. To serve an app to your users, deploy it to a hosting service such as AWS Amplify Hosting . A browser can’t add a SigV4 signature or a bearer token to the requests a page makes on its own, so the Session endpoint client in the bedrock-agentcore SDK can open a local endpoint on your machine. Your browser opens http://localhost:8088 , and the local endpoint adds your credentials to each request and WebSocket handshake before forwarding it. title: How Worldwide Express automated freight exceptions with Amazon Bedrock
abstract: Worldwide Express (part of ShipStation Global) had built something big: approximately $5 billion in systemwide revenue, over 75 less-than-truckload (LTL) carriers and more than 130,000 customers. But that same scale had a hidden cost. Every month, $15 million in free cash flow sat frozen, locked in billing exceptions no one had resolved yet. Each one had to be chased down by hand, carrier by carrier, with its own rules to check. Worldwide Express outsourced to a team that worked cases one at a time, calling customers and carriers for each dispute. The exceptions piled up, cash stayed stuck, and every order took longer to turn into money. Worldwide Express worked with AWS and LTM to build a multi-agentic AI solution with Amazon Bedrock that plugs directly into their transportation management system (TMS), SpeedShip. Six months after launch, the company reported a 75 percent reduction in active exceptions, a 4-week improvement in time-to-cash, $1M annual savings, and a one-time $10M free cash flow infusion. In this post, we describe the challenge, explain how Worldwide Express designed the multi-agent solution, and share the results. The challenge In LTL freight, roughly 14 percent of invoices fail the standard three-way match between the purchase order, the goods receipt, and the carrier invoice. When a match fails, the invoice enters exception handling. For Worldwide Express, exceptions fell into three categories: Line-item mismatches: Quantities or service codes that didn’t align with the shipment record. Pricing variances: The carrier billed a rate different from the contracted price. Unexpected accessorial charges: Liftgate fees, residential surcharges, or reweigh adjustments that weren’t on the original quote. Each exception triggered a five-step manual process: Identify the exception type by cross-referencing the invoice against the purchase order, goods receipt, and pricing. Research the root cause in vendor records. Send email to the carrier or warehouse with dispute details. Wait for a response. Execute the resolution in the TMS. With each carrier operating under its own tariff structure and dispute workflow, this process consumed most of the FinOps team’s bandwidth. Rule-based process automation (RPA) can handle structured, predictable workflows. However, exception resolution requires contextual judgment: interpreting a carrier’s accessorial policy, comparing charges against shipment data, and deciding validity given a carrier, exception type, and dollar amount. That variability is what made the problem a fit for the agentic AI framework. From assessment to production In June 2025, Worldwide Express engaged the AWS Business Transformation & Value Advisory team to identify 19 automation opportunities across the Order-to-Cash lifecycle. Knowing the business value of exceptions automation, Worldwide Express moved from assessment to production in less than 6 months. How it works The solution runs on AWS. Amazon Bedrock provides AI reasoning, and Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) is the engine. The design calls for fine-grained control over how each agent reasons, where decision boundaries sit, and how exceptions are routed between agents. Building the framework directly on Amazon EC2, with Amazon Bedrock providing inference, keeps that orchestration logic fully in the team’s hands and supports open source agent libraries. Production controls of business logic make each agent’s role, inputs, and decision boundaries explicit and auditable. In a billing-dispute workflow, every automated decision needs to be explainable. Agents When an invoice exception is detected, the system routes it to one of three specialized AI agents, each handling a specific type of billing dispute: Invoice Matching Agent finds the matching shipment record and flags what doesn’t line up. abstract: The ChatGPT desktop app is now available on Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US) , providing access to OpenAI’s frontier models through two components. Work completes complex, multi-step tasks and delivers review-ready results, and Codex is a coding agent for developing, testing, and reviewing software. This walkthrough is intended for organizations whose security architecture requires model inference to use AWS GovCloud (US) identities, endpoints, and Regional controls. It configures Codex to route model requests through Amazon Bedrock Mantle in us-gov-west-1 , where access can be governed using AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) and existing AWS GovCloud (US) network controls. Codex is the OpenAI coding agent for AI-powered software development. With GPT models powering inference, Codex introduces a new class of intelligence optimized for complex, long-horizon developer workflows. You can use the ChatGPT desktop app, the Codex CLI, and IDE integrations with Visual Studio Code, JetBrains, and Xcode. Model inference is routed through the Responses API on Amazon Bedrock. For customers with data residency requirements, processing stays within the Amazon Bedrock AWS Region that you select. You pay per token with no seat licenses and no per-developer commitments. Zero data retention (ZDR) is also supported. In this configurable mode, prompts and responses are processed without being written to durable storage by AWS or shared with model providers. This helps you protect sensitive information and meet stringent data-governance, privacy, and security requirements. This post walks through a controlled local deployment of the ChatGPT desktop app that sends model inference to Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US-West). The configuration uses API-mode sign-in, a managed device policy, a named AWS profile, and network restrictions. These restrictions allow access only to the approved Amazon Bedrock endpoint while disabling other external connections and network-enabled capabilities. The result is a deployment that an agency security team can test and document before approving broader use. Using AWS GovCloud (US) and following this guide do not, by themselves, authorize your workload. Your organization remains responsible for reviewing the selected model, AWS services, Region, endpoint, workstation controls, repositories, credentials, and data flows against its system security plan and authorization process. Solution overview You can use the ChatGPT desktop app in two ways: Work for larger tasks that need planning, research, files, and a finished result. Codex for technical work such as editing code, running tests, and reviewing pull requests. The ChatGPT desktop app runs on an organization-managed computer through the desktop app or CLI. It uses the configured AWS credentials to securely send requests to the Amazon Bedrock Mantle endpoint in us-gov-west-1 . Because this setup uses AWS directly, ChatGPT workspace rules and user roles don’t control it. The main security controls are the computer’s policies and the AWS identity and permissions being used. Walkthrough The configuration has three main steps: set up authentication, set up the ChatGPT desktop app configuration files, and then launch, initialize, and verify the deployment. abstract: This event summary was created by Claude with light editing by Tim O’Reilly, based on a transcript of the event. On October 15, 2026, Tim O’Reilly hosted Andrew Odewahn, CTO of O’Reilly Media, for an hour-long episode of Live with Tim O’Reilly , the interview series streamed live on the O’Reilly learning platform. Andrew has been at O’Reilly for many years, starting as an author, then building tools for the company’s platform, then eventually as CTO and head of engineering. Over the past year, his team has been building what the company calls Expert Intelligence , a suite of tools that connects an AI agent to an organization’s own systems, gives it a skill file describing how to reason about what it finds there, and grounds its analysis in the practitioner frameworks of the O’Reilly library. Andrew described the work in a recent Radar piece, “ Building Organizational Intelligence .” Tim and Andrew’s interview was organized around a presentation in two parts, the first on the research agent and the second on the system Andrew’s team built for reviewing what it produces, with discussion in between and audience questions throughout. Tim framed the conversation by asking a question he said Andrew’s work helps to answer: Most of the AI story is about efficiency, doing the same work faster. What does it look like for an organization to get smarter? Building the research agent Andrew’s research agent emerged from a personal need rather than a strategy. He wanted to know the status of a project, for example, how long a migration from RabbitMQ to Pub/Sub would take. This is the kind of question every engineer dreads but every engineering leader has to answer. He also had a broader concern. A single person being good at AI isn’t the same as an organization being good at it. He built his agent in four steps. He mapped the organization’s information systems as a hierarchy, connected them via MCP, wrote a skill telling the agent how to use them, and finally added the Expert Intelligence layer. The map of the sources of truth in the engineering organization’s workflows was what made the rest work. Andrew put them in order and explained to the model how they relate: Strategic goals and feature priorities live in Productboard. Those become epics, sprints, and stories in Jira. Stories become code in GitHub. A service catalog describes the roughly 300 services that make up the O’Reilly platform and who owns them, and observability tools show how those services perform against their SLOs. The skill also had to encode local quirks. Some teams mark an epic as finished with an end date, while others consider it done when every ticket is closed. Andrew also told the agent it was a research agent, not a coding agent, and that its job was to write reports. Connecting everything through MCP was, in his words, “the most completely tedious step of the whole process.” Productboard had no MCP server at the time, so he wrote a wrapper. Later, when Tim asked how another company could repeat the work with a different set of tools, Andrew suggested starting from the vendor list. Export it from your procurement system, ask the model what products those vendors make and which would hold information relevant to the questions you care about, and have it put them in order. O’Reilly product managers are now turning this process into a skill for the forthcoming Expert Intelligence Skills Hub. One audience member asked whether MCP was really the right tool for internal knowledge, compared with semantic search. As Andrew pointed out, sometimes anything is better than nothing. Ultimately, what you want is to give the model the ability to search across your systems. title: This Week in AI: Agents Rewrite the Rules
abstract: AI agents dominated the news this week, from security exploits that unfolded in hours to new tools that let agents shop, manage transactions, and conduct scientific research. On the latest episode of This Week in AI , host Vicki Reyzelman of Akamai examined how these developments are testing existing security practices and creating new opportunities for businesses and researchers. AI attacks are outpacing traditional security responses AI is changing how attackers find and exploit vulnerabilities. A supply chain attack involving ARTEX , an open source agentic AI penetration-testing framework, helped attackers reach more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants through a ConnectWise compromise. The incident raised concerns about OAuth authentication and the limitations of conventional identity protections when autonomous agents interact with enterprise systems. A more immediate threat came from PHP2Shell , two vulnerabilities rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale that could allow attackers to execute code on vulnerable web servers without authentication. CISA urged immediate patching following the October 21 disclosure. Researchers also documented attackers using AI agents to obtain password hashes and MFA secrets from a European government system within two hours. The speed of exploitation leaves organizations little time to investigate threats before responding, especially smaller businesses with limited security resources. Security teams can no longer rely on manual review alone. They need automated detection and response, tighter access controls, and network segmentation to limit what compromised agents can reach. But monitoring autonomous agents is challenging. Researchers from METR and Redwood Research identified weaknesses in an earlier version of OpenAI’s internal monitoring system, including one that could allow hundreds of agent actions to be concealed. OpenAI says it has patched vulnerabilities affecting production safeguards, although the researchers haven’t independently evaluated those changes. The debate over AI safety is also extending beyond technical safeguards. Anthropic proposed federal AI safety legislation , while Google DeepMind employees resigned over the company’s military AI work. Both developments illustrate the growing pressure on AI companies to establish clearer rules for how their technology is developed and used. The transition to agents brings new challenges Retailers are taking different approaches to autonomous shopping. Walmart introduced an Agent Gateway that lets approved agents shop within customer-defined spending limits and approval requirements. Amazon has restricted some third-party shopping agents, while banks including Morgan Stanley and Bank of America are limiting agent access to customer accounts. The disagreement goes beyond security. Retailers that depend on advertising and product recommendations have an incentive to keep shoppers on their websites. As more purchases begin with agents, companies will have to reconsider how they maintain customer relationships. Anthropic is testing a different approach to agent oversight. Claude’s auto mode is becoming the default for Pro, Max, and Team users, allowing automated checks to approve routine actions and block risky ones. Anthropic also contributed its Agent Skills format to the Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation. More than 70 platforms have adopted the standard, with over a million skills published. Shared formats could make workflows easier to reuse across products, although organizations still need to control which actions those workflows can perform. title: Who Governs What an Agent Learns?
abstract: The following article originally appeared on Tim O’Brien’s Medium blog and is being republished here with the author’s permission. I think we’re missing something in the conversation about agent security. We keep asking whether an agent has the right “identity” and “credentials.” Whether its credentials expire fast enough. Whether it can access a database or perform a particular task. Those questions matter. But they leave a much harder question underneath: Does the agent have permission to conceive of the situation in that way? As agents retain memories and acquire new skills, we need mechanisms that govern changes to the world model they can perceive and act on—and prevent those changes from silently expanding their authority. (Governing ontological change while preserving the boundaries of delegated authority.) An Interesting Morning by the Beach (AI assist from OpenAI) Agent security needs semantic and epistemic governance: Mechanisms that govern the model of the world an agent may act on, the evidence it may accept, and who may approve changes to either. An agent can learn without automatically gaining authority to act on everything it learns. These systems don’t need “awareness” to create this problem (and discussions of consciousness are unhelpful science fiction). They can retain information, revise procedures, and use what they have learned in subsequent work. That learning may happen through memory or updated skills while the underlying language model remains unchanged. We are responsible for governing what that learning allows them to do. Flatland gives me a way to explain why In Edwin Abbott’s novella , a Square lives in a two-dimensional world. A visiting Sphere introduces him to a third dimension. At first, the Square struggles to make sense of it. His familiar categories cannot explain what he is encountering. Eventually, his conception of the world changes. What interests me is the difference between simply acquiring another fact and changing the framework through which facts make sense. An agent’s ontology ( Gruber’s definition ) supplies an explicit framework of concepts and relationships. What counts as a customer? A contract? An emergency? How are those things connected? It is part of the model of the world we give the system to work with. And when an agent’s decisions depend on that framework, changing it can change the agent’s effective authority. We have already seen agents change what their environment means During the OpenAI evaluations associated with the Hugging Face incident, agents repurposed Artifactory, a system for storing and retrieving software packages, as a message board. They encoded messages in directory names, discovered other agents, shared information, and began assigning work to one another. METR reports that the main channel could be created with the minimal permissions needed to install packages ( read METR’s investigation ). A package cache became a “mailbox.” Other agent runs became “collaborators.” Messages became “assignments.” The popular story is that these agents “broke out” of a system, but they did what agents do well these days—they learned and adapted. This wasn’t so much about permissions as it was about an autonomous system adapting its operating model to achieve a result. (Thankfully no one asked it to make paperclips.) That is the operating-model change I’m concerned about. The agents discovered relationships and possibilities the intended environment hadn’t accounted for, then acted on them. The resulting collaboration helped coordinate attacks on Hugging Face infrastructure. ( Read OpenAI’s account .) We need mechanisms that distinguish discovering a possible use from being authorized to adopt it. Access to shared infrastructure must not automatically confer authority to establish a communications network or accept instructions from whoever appears there. title: Eating disorders are on the rise. GLP-1s could make things worse.
abstract: GLP-1 weight-loss drugs are one of the biggest biotech breakthroughs of the last decade. But to some clinical psychologists, they can represent something more sinister—a potential trigger for eating disorders. A new report suggests that the global incidence of anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa shot up between 1990 and 2023—by a whopping 71%. By 2023, there were an estimated 18.1 million people living with one of these two disorders. What’s worse is that the number is likely to be much higher than that once we factor in other eating disorders. And, disturbingly, those in the field are already starting to see GLP-1 weight-loss drugs exacerbating the issue. Cheri Levinson is a clinical psychologist at the University of Louisville in Kentucky who has specialized in eating disorders for almost 20 years. She says she’s now seeing more patients with more severe symptoms than at any other time in her career, and that many of them are misusing GLP-1s. “This is the worst I’ve seen things,” she says. Eating disorders are mental health conditions in which people’s eating behaviors impact their health. They include anorexia nervosa (defined by a fear of weight gain), bulimia nervosa (in which people binge and purge), binge eating disorder, and others. It’s thought that some people have a genetic predisposition to certain eating disorders, but that some external factor is what triggers their onset. That might be stress, or social pressure to be skinny. Often, simply restricting food intake can trigger an eating disorder, says Levinson. Eating disorders—along with the pressure to look thin—were already prevalent in the 1990s (the heroin chic era springs to mind). To find out how things might have changed since then, Ruhai Bai at the Children’s Hospital of Nanjing Medical University in China and his colleagues pulled together data from studies and surveys conducted on populations around the world. The team used statistical models to fill in any data gaps. That research allowed the researchers to estimate the annual incidence of two eating disorders—anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa—for each of 204 countries and territories between 1990 and 2023. They also estimated the impact those disorders had on global health by calculating their disability-adjusted life years (one DALY represents a year of healthy life lost). The findings, published in JAMA Psychiatry on Wednesday, are unsettling. Between 1990 and 2023, there was a 71% increase in the incidence of those two eating disorders, the team found. Those conditions had a huge impact on global health, too. In 2023, they “cost the world the equivalent of about 3.83 million years of healthy life,” says Bai. Bai and his colleagues expect these figures to continue to rise. In 2023, an estimated 18.1 million people had either anorexia nervosa or bulimia nervosa; by 2050, the team predict, the two conditions could affect 21.8 million people. It gets worse. Those two conditions represent less than half of all eating disorders, says Levinson, who was not involved in Bai’s study. The true impact of these disorders is “probably three times the rate that they’re reporting,” she says. Bai and his colleagues didn’t explore the reasons for this rise (although Bai points out that it can’t be entirely explained by population growth). So how did we get here? Social media may have played a role. “Social media comparisons, influencers, challenges, diet trends can all be precipitating … events for an eating disorder,” says Cynthia Bulik, a clinical psychologist at the University of North Carolina, who was not involved in the new study. Bulik has been studying and treating eating disorders since the early 1980s. “Between 1990 and 2023 there has clearly been an upsurge of those types of environmental exposures,” she says. title: Consumer Appetite for Personal AI Goes Mainstream
abstract: This article is brought to you by Qualcomm Technologies . For many consumers, much of the promise and appeal of AI is personal. Consumers are looking past generic tools and want to know how these technologies will help them in their daily lives. These trends coincide with the advent of new classes of wearable devices that, in addition to being able to leverage powerful frontier models, feature built-in intelligence that understand the context of a user. Where are they? What are they seeing and hearing? What are their habits, their preferences, their schedules? It’s an astonishing pivot, from passive accessories that served mostly to send users smartphone notifications to proactive, intelligent companions. The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI. And it shifts the focus toward you, the user. These new technologies are exciting. But what do consumers really want? A Personal AI report , commissioned by Qualcomm Technologies, built on a survey of more than 12,000 people across key geographies worldwide (the U.S., U.K., Germany, India, Brazil, and China) focused on the rise of personal AI in intelligent wearables looks deeply at these developments. The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI. Survey respondents are less interested in single devices and are responding more to the idea of connected ecosystems. As people expand their roster of devices, it only makes sense. Instead of relying entirely on a smartphone and a laptop, respondents also have connected technology in their cars, as well as intelligent wearables like smartwatches, smart glasses, hearables, and other wearables like rings, pins, and pendants. They want those devices to work in concert, and the way to do that is to decentralize any single one of them. Instead, the AI agent that knows the user and works across all of those devices becomes the unifying factor. Consider a typical workday: A user’s watch detects it is time to leave for a meeting and, with permission, their AI agent factors in calendar details, real-time traffic and battery status across their devices. In the car, it suggests the best route and briefs them on their meeting agenda. As they arrive, smart glasses surface a discreet reminder, such as the meeting location or the name of a new contact, while the phone stays in their pocket. No one device has to do everything; each plays the role it is best suited for, coordinated by a personal AI agent that understands the user’s context and acts only at the user’s direction. With this in mind, simply adding more hardware to the mix isn’t sufficient. Even though respondents will be open to new form factors, they’ll demand more from their ecosystem of devices. They’ll be sensitive to points of friction and needless complexity, and they’ll require each new device to bring something new to the table — “incremental intelligence, convenience, or contextual awareness that their existing devices cannot deliver on their own what the report,” reads the report. The usage trends are up. The report found that those who own wearables are already using AI frequently (60 percent use it at least weekly), which indicates that it’s becoming less of a fun experiment for early adopters and more of a critical mass habit. The “always-on” nature of intelligent wearables appears to be winning respondents, too. The report found the following statistics on average continuous wear among users: True wireless earbuds – 3 hours Wireless headphones – 3 hours Smart glasses – 5 hours Audio glasses – 6 hours Smartwatches – 9 hours Smart rings, necklaces and pendants – 8 hours Consumers want AI that is personal and understands their context — they’re looking for smooth, intuitive experiences that are marked by privacy, security, and user control. title: Think you can save the Hubble Space Telescope? NASA wants to know.
abstract: The Hubble Space Telescope still shines in the eyes of astronomers after 36 years in orbit, but it is not as nimble as it once was. Left alone, the observatory will plunge back into the atmosphere in the early-to-mid-2030s, closing the book on one of the most famous scientific instruments of the century. NASA last raised the orbit of Hubble in 2002, when the Space Shuttle Columbia visited the observatory for a servicing mission. The final shuttle servicing flight in 2009 did not reboost the telescope's orbit, and with the retirement of the shuttle fleet two years later, Hubble has steadily lost altitude with no way to stave off eventual destruction. The space agency released a Request For Information (RFI) on Thursday asking commercial companies for ideas on how to reboost, service, or a controlled disposal of Hubble. Responses are due November 30. Specifically, NASA is looking for information about companies' current and near-term capabilities for capturing Hubble and boosting it to an altitude of at least 373 miles (600 km), enhancing the telescope's performance through, or guiding Hubble to a controlled reentry. abstract: An official extension for Anthropic’s Claude model was backdoored and threatened as many as 5,000 developers' machines, multiple sources reported Friday. title: Over 25% of people lie to get antibiotics—and their lies aren't even good
abstract: A significant number of patients in the US lie to their doctors to get antibiotics they likely don't need, according to two new studies. While that may not be a startling revelation, the studies drills down on the phenomenon, finding that the lies patients tell are generally bad ones—and yet, they work almost all the time. In the two linked studies published Friday in JAMA Network Open, a team of researchers led by Alistair Thorpe at the University of Utah analyzed online survey data from over 1,000 adults. They found that over a quarter of people reported having lied to a clinician at least once to get an antibiotic prescription for themselves or a child in their care. Patients lied by either exaggerating symptoms, making up symptoms, or—most often—both. But interestingly, the lies people told to get antibiotics involved making up or exaggerating symptoms of infections that wouldn't be treated with antibiotics. For example, the most common falsehoods were symptoms associated with colds, such as fever, cough, and sore throat. That's despite the fact that colds are caused by viruses, not bacteria—which antibiotics treat. Read full article Comments

title: Basically no one is using AI agents for their DoorDash orders
abstract: As AI tools and agents have continued their march across all aspects of digital life, many companies are trying to use LLMs to improve the experience of purchasing goods and services on the Internet. Thus far, though, a vanishingly small number of people seem to be taking advantage of those capabilities, at least when it comes to using the popular food delivery app DoorDash with an outside AI agent. In a third-quarter earnings call Thursday , DoorDash co-founder and CEO Tony Xu responded to an analyst question by noting that "AI agents are generating several hundred orders [on DoorDash] across the time that they've been up and running." In a marked understatement, Xu called this a "very low use case" for a company that handled just shy of 1 billion orders total in the third quarter of 2026 alone. Speaking generally, Xu said he sees the potential for AI agents to be genuinely helpful for "long consideration purchases" and major decisions where agents would be "doing work on your behalf proactively in the background." However, Xu added, "when it comes to a task that's as simple as ordering food, we tend to see that come directly to DoorDash." Read full article Comments

title: Rare meteorite from Mars gives us a view into its ancient crust
abstract: Crater counts tell us that most of the Martian surface is more than 3 billion years old, but pieces of Mars we have on Earth tell a different story. The three main classes of Martian meteorites—shergottites, nakhlites, and chassignites—are all 2.4 billion years old or younger. Until now, only two genuinely ancient Martian meteorites were known: Allan Hills 84001, found in Antarctica, and a jumbled rock from northwest Africa nicknamed Black Beauty. Now we have a third one. A team led by Yang Liu, a planetary scientist at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, has shown that a Martian meteorite called Teghaza 001, found in the Sahara Desert in Mali in 2022, formed at least 4.1 billion years ago. “It's very old and similar to some of the oldest rocks on Earth,” Liu says. A filtered collection “We don't fully understand why old Martian rocks are so rare on Earth," Liu said. Part of the answer may lie in how a piece of Mars gets here. It takes a large impact to launch a rock off the planet, and not every rock can survive that. “If the impact hits into loose powder, it may not get cemented to become a rock and fly off Mars' gravity,” Liu said. “So the natural impact already acts as a filter. Weak rocks do not make it off Mars.” Read full article Comments

title: 2027 Nissan Rogue Hybrid: Drives like an EV, but there's no plug involved
abstract: Nissan provided flights from Washington, DC, to Santa Barbara, California, and accommodation so Ars could drive the Rogue Hybrid. Ars does not accept paid editorial content. Nissan has a new version of its bestselling Rogue SUV, and it’s launching the model here with the latest version of its e-Power hybrid system, which Ars tested in February. Most hybrid cars you can buy today are parallel hybrids, which means that they have an internal combustion engine and an electric motor, both of which drive some or all of the wheels—everything works in parallel. But there’s another approach. Instead of connecting the engine to the wheels via a transmission, it can act as a generator and charge the traction battery, which in turn powers the electric motor. Since the engine and motor work in series, this is known as a series hybrid. That’s mostly how the Chevrolet Volt worked. As does Honda’s hybrid CR-V . Well, mostly; engineers worked out it was more efficient for those cars' gasoline engines to directly drive the wheels at highway speeds, something that to this day makes a certain subset of hybrid car enthusiasts irrationally angry. If you know anyone like that in your life, send them to wherever the nearest Nissan dealership is, because the 2027 Rogue Hybrid is exactly what they’ve been asking for. Series hybrids Under the hood, with its crisp shut line and slim horizontal lights that give me something of a Range Rover vibe, there’s a 1.5 L, three-cylinder turbocharged direct-injection engine that generates 148 hp (110 kW). It only revs to 5,200 rpm because it’s optimized to charge the battery, not cope with the various loads of an engine connected to a gearbox and the wheels. That also allows the engine to operate at a rather impressive 42 percent thermal efficiency—we would need to look at Formula 1 engines to find higher. Read full article Comments

title: Review: You Can See Everything blurs the view of Elizabeth Holmes' deceit
abstract: In 2015, biomedical entrepreneur Elizabeth Holmes was Silicon Valley's golden girl, lauded as the youngest and richest self-made female billionaire thanks to the company she founded, Theranos, which was valued at $9 billion at the height of its success. Then it all came crashing down when accusations of fraud surfaced about the company's signature blood-testing device, culminating in a sensational trial. Holmes was convicted on four counts and sentenced to 11 years in prison. Holmes is back in the headlines thanks to a new film, You Can See Everything , which depicts the final days before Holmes, having exhausted her appeals , went to prison. Co-directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim , it's a surreal, absurdist piece that has largely been received with gushing enthusiasm and no small amount of hype, with some declaring it the best film of the year. A few contrarian voices have emerged over the past week with much-needed reality checks, but there's no denying the film is destined to be an awards-season darling. Pardon me for joining the buzzkills, but I cannot in good conscience jump on the You Can See Everything bandwagon. Sure, it has its moments, and the second half is highly entertaining, but there's nothing here to warrant all the breathless hyperbole. For all their much-touted access, Oppenheim and Fielder have produced a surprisingly shallow film that runs in circles, yielding very little fresh or novel insight—into Holmes, personally, or much else. title: 모두가 함께 성장하는 기술 축제, NAVER Engineering Day 10년의 여정
abstract: 기술은 혼자 완성되지 않습니다. ​ 한 사람이 발견한 문제와 해결 과정이 동료에게 전해지고, 그 경험이 또 다른 시도와 개선으로 이어질 때 조직의 기술은 앞으로 나아갑니다. ​ NAVER Engineering Day는 이런 믿음에서 출발했습니다. 2016년, 실무에서 얻은 개발 경험과 새로운 기술 및 플랫폼을 도입하며 배운 점을 나누는 사내 개발자 행사로 시작해 올해 10주년을 맞았습니다. 그동안 Engineering Day는 발표자가 정리한 지식을 듣는 자리를 넘어, 서로의 경험을 연결하고 각자의 업무 문제를 함께 해결하는 장으로 꾸준히 확장돼 왔습니다. ​ 특히 AI가 특정 직군의 전문 도구를 넘어 일하는 방식 전반을 바꾸기 시작하면서 기술을 나눈다는 말의 의미도 달라졌습니다. 중요한 것은 새로운 도구를 아는 데 그치지 않고, 내 문제에 적용해 보고 막히는 지점을 동료와 함께 풀어 보는 경험입니다. ​ 10주년 Engineering Day는 이러한 변화에 맞춰 전 직군이 함께 온라인 세션, 오프라인 워크숍, AI 오픈 코칭데이로 이어지는 4일간의 여정으로 진행됐습니다. ​ 10년 동안 이어진 동료의 경험 Engineering Day의 중심에는 늘 구성원이 직접 준비한 이야기가 있었습니다. 완성된 기술을 소개하는 데 그치지 않고, 실제 업무에서 마주한 문제와 선택, 시행착오, 그 과정에서 얻은 교훈을 나눴습니다. ​ 주제의 범위도 기술 환경과 함께 넓어졌습니다. 백엔드, 데이터, 모바일을 비롯한 개발 분야부터 AI 도구를 활용한 업무 개선과 협업 방식까지, 서로 다른 역할의 구성원이 각자의 관점에서 경험을 꺼내 놓았습니다. 발표를 통해 한 사람의 경험은 여러 동료가 다시 활용할 수 있는 지식이 됐고, 질문과 대화는 다음 실험의 출발점이 됐습니다. ​ Engineering Day가 10년 동안 이어질 수 있었던 힘은 거창한 구호보다 이 단순한 선순환에 있습니다. 먼저 경험한 동료가 기꺼이 나누고, 다른 동료가 자신의 업무에 맞게 다시 시도하며, 그 결과를 또다시 공유하는 문화입니다. ​ 서로의 경험을 발견하는 온라인 세션 첫날에는 구성원들이 직접 준비한 온라인 세션이 열렸습니다. 발표자들은 성공 사례만 소개하지 않았습니다. 문제를 어떻게 정의했는지, 어떤 선택지 사이에서 고민했는지, 실제 적용 과정에서 무엇이 기대와 달랐는지까지 공유했습니다. 덕분에 참가자들은 익숙한 분야의 지식을 확장하는 동시에 평소 접하기 어려웠던 다른 직무의 문제 해결 방식도 살펴볼 수 있었습니다. ​ 온라인 세션은 기술을 '아는 것'에서 시작하는 단계였습니다. 이어진 프로그램에서는 이 지식을 직접 다뤄 보고 각자의 업무와 연결했습니다. ​ 더 나아가 네이버 내부에서만 그치지 않고, 다음 주 부터 Engineering Day에서 발표된 30여개의 온라인 세션을 D2를 통해서 공개할 예정입니다. ​ 두 손으로 따라하며 내 것으로 만드는 워크숍 ​ 이어서 오프라인 워크숍을 진행했습니다. 참가자들은 설명을 듣는 데 머물지 않고, 준비된 예제와 각자의 과제를 직접 다루며 기술을 적용했습니다. ​ 워크숍에서는 개발자를 위한 심화 기술뿐 아니라 비개발 직군의 AI 협업, 디자이너와 개발자의 연결 등 다양한 역할에서 활용할 수 있는 주제를 함께 다뤘습니다. 같은 도구도 맡은 업무와 해결하려는 문제에 따라 쓰임이 달라졌고, 참가자들은 실습 과정에서 동료와 의견을 나누며 각자에게 맞는 활용 방식을 찾았습니다. ​ 이 과정은 기술 공유의 효과가 좋은 설명만으로 완성되지 않는다는 점을 보여 줬습니다. 직접 실행해 보고, 예상과 다른 결과를 확인하고, 그 이유를 함께 짚어 볼 때 지식은 비로소 자신의 경험이 됩니다. ​ 각자의 경험으로 함께 고민하는 AI 오픈 코칭데이 마지막 날에는 올해 처음으로 AI 오픈 코칭데이를 열었습니다. 온라인 세션에서 개념을 익히고 워크숍에서 실습했더라도, 실제 업무에 적용하려는 순간에는 새로운 질문이 생깁니다. 어디서 시작해야 할지, 문제를 어떻게 나눠야 할지, 현재 방식에서 무엇을 바꿔야 할지 막막할 수 있습니다. ​ AI 오픈 코칭데이는 정해진 강의를 듣는 대신 참가자가 자신의 업무 고민을 가져와 동료 코치와 함께 풀어 보는 방식으로 진행했습니다. 참가자는 문제 상황을 설명하고 직접 도구를 실행했으며, 코치는 정답을 건네기보다 문제를 구체화하고 다음 시도를 설계할 수 있도록 도왔습니다. ​ 코칭 과정에서 배운 사람과 가르치는 사람의 경계도 자연스럽게 흐려졌습니다. 코치들은 서로 다른 접근법에서 새로운 관점을 얻었고, 참가자는 자신의 문제를 말로 정리하고 직접 해결 과정을 밟으며 다음 단계로 나아갈 실마리를 찾았습니다. 한 사람의 질문이 주변 동료의 배움이 되고, 한 사람의 해결 경험이 다시 다른 사람에게 전해지는 순간이었습니다. ​ 다음 10년에도, 기술은 사람 사이에서 이어집니다. 10주년 Engineering Day는 지난 시간을 기념하는 행사인 동시에 앞으로의 기술 공유 방식을 살펴보는 자리였습니다. 발표를 통해 발견하고, 워크숍에서 직접 시도하고, 코칭을 통해 내 문제에 연결하는 흐름은 기술 학습이 일회성 콘텐츠 소비에 머물지 않도록 했습니다. ​ AI 시대에는 도구의 변화가 빠른 만큼 모든 답을 미리 준비하기 어렵습니다. 그래서 완성된 답을 전달하는 것만큼 문제를 함께 정의하고, 시도한 과정을 나누며, 서로의 시행착오를 다음 출발점으로 만드는 일이 중요합니다. ​ NAVER Engineering Day의 지난 10년은 동료의 경험이 조직의 지식으로 이어지는 시간이었습니다. 다음 10년에도 NAVER는 각자의 자리에서 발견한 문제와 배움을 연결하고, 함께 더 나은 해답을 만들어 가겠습니다. ​ D2에서 이어갈 Engineering Day의 다양한 기술 이야기에도 많은 관심 부탁드립니다.

title: Read, Allocate, Route: Role-Coupled Tokenization for Pixel-Space Generative Transformers
abstract: Pixel-space generative Transformers typically use one token per image patch, so capturing finer detail requires more tokens and makes global attention increasingly expensive. We observe that finer detail does not necessarily require more global communication: low-frequency structure benefits from global exchange, while high-frequency detail can be modeled locally. Based on this insight, we introduce SpecSlot, a pixel-space rectified-flow Transformer that decouples output detail from the length of the global attention sequence. SpecSlot expands each spatial anchor into multiple slots, each assigned a disjoint band of DCT coefficients; this separates anchor density from spectral subdivision. Only the lowest-frequency slot from each anchor participates in global attention, while all slots interact locally. This allows the model to increase spectral detail without enlarging the global sequence. A spatial head further adds a local correction to the spectral prediction, while the generative state, target, and loss remain in pixel space. On ImageNet-256, SpecSlot achieves a comparable final FID to a FLOPs-matched JiT control while converging faster. On ImageNet-512, it improves FID by 2.84 over the control with 3.9% fewer FLOPs, and comes within only 0.69 FID of JiT-B/16 at 38.2% lower cost. On text-to-image generation, SpecSlot surpasses JiT-B/8 on DPG-Bench by 1.06 at 40.6% lower forward cost.

title: Retrieval as Traversal: Value-Indexed Memory for Stateful Long-Context Agents
abstract: Long-context models repeatedly solve closely related retrieval problems. Attention or global retrieval can retain large stores, but each forward pass again searches for what matters. Recurrent compression avoids this search only by deciding earlier what information to preserve. Neither mechanism directly exploits that useful memories at neighbouring retrieval steps may substantially overlap. We propose an alternative in which retrieval is a persistent local traversal through an address space. We separate a memory's content from its address. Utility is defined by the information revealed by retrieving the content, while geometry determines only how cheaply that information can be reached. This leads to a cost-regularised indexing objective that preserves information value inside local neighbourhoods while charging for every memory made locally accessible. Its marginal-value form gives both attractive and exclusion pressures. Thus, complementary memories should be co-retrievable when the additional value exceeds retrieval cost, whereas redundant memories should not occupy the same retrieval set solely because they are individually useful. As a proof of principle, we test only the simplest fixed-geometry instance on MiniGrid Memory. A persistent local traversal head reaches $0.95$ mean return after $0.59$M training steps with a five-token context, compared with $0.94$M for Gaussian absolute addressing and more than $2$M for categorical absolute addressing. The experiment does not test learned geometry or repeated retrieval. Instead, it motivates the hypothesis that stateful retrieval may be easier to learn than stateless. To test the full proposed method further experimentation is necessary.

title: Numerical Integration on Bounded Domains via Learned Reflected Diffusions
abstract: We study high-dimensional integration on bounded convex domains. Given a non-negative integrand $r$, the goal is to estimate $Z=\int_{D}r(x)\,\mathrm dx$ on $D\subset\mathbb R^d$. Standard Quasi-Monte Carlo does not adapt its evaluation points to the integrand, while effective importance sampling requires a proposal that captures its concentration. Learned diffusion samplers can supply such a proposal, but existing methods are formulated on $\mathbb R^d$ and do not respect the domain constraint $x\in D$. We instead build the proposal from reflected dynamics that stay in $D$ by construction. A reflected diffusion progressively transforms the target distribution toward the uniform distribution on $D$, and a neural score model is trained to reverse this process. A change-of-measure formula for reflected diffusions yields a training objective without additional boundary terms and an unbiased importance-sampling estimator of $Z$. For non-smooth integrands, where reparameterization gradients may be undefined or uninformative, we derive a REINFORCE estimator of the training gradient using Gaussian proposal densities before reflection, without evaluating reflected transition densities or differentiating $r$. We evaluate on numerous synthetic targets and real-world problems, demonstrating strong performance of the proposed method, as well as favorable scaling with the dimension of the problem and the number of points used for the Monte Carlo estimate.

title: Prefix Executability: Evaluating Tool-Using Agents Beyond Final Success
abstract: Tool-use benchmarks often score agents by final task success, but terminal outcomes can obscure whether the intermediate tool-call trajectory was executable. We propose prefix executability as a trajectory-level evaluation protocol for tool-using agents. The protocol measures whether every prefix of a predicted tool-call sequence remains executable under tool schemas, state preconditions, and data dependencies, and summarizes reliability using Prefix Executability Curves (PEC), First-Error Depth (FED), Trajectory Executability Rate (TER), horizon-normalized AUC-PEC, and Recovery Rate (RR). We instantiate the protocol on stratified samples from BFCL-v3 multi-turn and ToolSandbox, and on the complete Airline/Retail base splits of $τ^3$-bench. We observe that outcome-only and prefix-level rankings diverge: agents whose execution is conditioned on an unverified plan often achieve higher point-estimate final success than non-plan-conditioned baselines while substantially lowering TER and AUC-PEC. These divergences are precisely the failure modes that prefix executability is designed to expose: they reveal whether apparent success rests on an executable trajectory, where invalidity first enters, and whether success follows recovery from an earlier failure. As a validation intervention, explicit pre-execution plan checking can improve executable-prefix survival while maintaining competitive terminal success. These results show that final success alone is insufficient for evaluating tool-use agents and that prefix-level executability provides an actionable reliability signal for comparing agents, diagnosing failures, and assessing validation mechanisms.

title: EnvOS: Auditing Computer-Use Agents When the World Moves On : Phenomenon-Based Task Construction, Certification, and Evidence-Based Evaluation
abstract: Computer-use agents built on large language models (LLMs) work in software that can change while they act: an appointment moves, a policy is revised, a record is updated. Testing agents under such changes is harder than it looks. When an agent fails, the cause may be the agent, but it may also be a change that did not fire as intended, an update the agent never received, or a grader that scored the episode wrongly. We introduce EnvOS, a framework for building and certifying environments that change mid-task. Before any agent runs, EnvOS checks that each change fires correctly, that the task remains solvable, and that the grader separates correct from incorrect behavior; after each run, separate code re-checks the verdict from archived evidence. We apply it to stale information, where a value the agent has already seen changes before the agent acts on it. In clinic booking, Claude Opus 5 succeeds on 0/16 tasks when nothing extra is shown, 2/16 when reminded to re-check the source, and 15/16 when the updated value is shown; the gain over the reminder holds after correcting for all tests (p = 0.00293). In insurance-claim approval, Opus 5 re-checks on its own and succeeds on 10/10, whereas Claude Sonnet 5 rises from 1/10 to 9/10 when the current policy is shown again, a gain significant in its pre-registered test but not after correcting for all tests. Whether an agent caught a change thus varied with the model and the interface. We also stress-test the grading itself: on corrupted episodes designed blind from the rules, the EnvOS pipeline accepted none of 26 as clean, and on an externally generated set it caught 25 of 39, against 4 for simple log checks. Because every EnvOS environment is generated from a seed and graded by an audited automatic verifier, the same environments are natural candidates for training agents with reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards.

title: Escaping Path Mirages in Offline Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning remains challenging in stochastic long-horizon settings, where compounding value estimation errors hinder reliable goal reaching. While prior methods have sought to address this challenge through various approaches, a key challenge remains path mirage, where agents overcommit to spuriously successful trajectories in offline datasets induced by stochasticity, often leading to failure on difficult tasks. To address this issue, we propose Branch-aware Graph Planning (BGP), which captures stochastic branching structures by identifying high-variability points as graph nodes and designing goal-conditioned edges with segmented learning to avoid unreliable branches and reduce unnecessary stochasticity along paths. As a result, BGP enables reliable goal reaching even in highly stochastic long-horizon environments, and experiments on diverse OGBench tasks show that it substantially outperforms prior state-of-the-art offline goal-conditioned RL methods. Our implementation is available at https://umlic.github.io/papers/BGP/.

title: Coupled Guidance for Flow Matching
abstract: Guidance methods are essential tools for steering the generation process in diffusion models, improving the generalizability of stochastic robotic controllers and enabling high-quality controlled image synthesis. Despite strong parallels between flow-matching and diffusion, integrating guidance into flow-matching models remains quite challenging. Recent work has proposed general guidance frameworks for flow-matching, however, they are direct adaptations of diffusion guidance methods and can prove unstable. In this work, we conduct a theoretical analysis of guidance in flow-matching and show that a naive translation of diffusion-based guidance to flow-matching breaks the coupling distribution used during training, resulting in weaker control over sampling accuracy. Building on this insight, we propose Coupled Guidance, a flow-matching-specific guidance mechanism derived from a geometric perspective that leverages the coupling structure inherent to flow-matching training. To validate the effectiveness of our approach, we conduct extensive experimentation on a custom robotic collision avoidance task using ManiSkill3, four robotic dexterous manipulation tasks from the Adroit benchmark, and three image generation tasks, namely inpainting, super-resolution, and deblurring, using the ImageNet-128 and CelebA-HQ-256 datasets. Our findings show that our framework improves sample quality and guidance stability across all tasks, without imposing any additional overhead.

title: Mind The Gap (MTG-AD): Dataset and Fine-grained Evaluation for End-to-End Inline Audio Descriptions
abstract: Audio descriptions (AD) are essential for making visual media accessible to blind and low-vision (BLV) users. While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) offer a scalable solution for generating audio descriptions on-demand, their performance on ``inline'' audio descriptions -- which must fit within existing silences in a video -- remains under-explored, particularly for diverse user-generated content (UGC). We present a comprehensive investigation into MLLM-generated inline audio descriptions. First, we introduce MTG-AD, a professionally annotated dataset of 36 hours of videos, each averaging $\sim$5 mins. and 8k+ descriptions in total, co-created by paired blind and sighted AD professionals to provide a high-quality benchmark for this task. Second, we propose MTG-AD-Eval, an evaluation framework based on audio description expert guidelines that provides fine-grained, reference-free actionable metrics for model improvement. Crucially, our framework evaluates the end-to-end task: it renders the generated scripts into audio tracks to assess their fit within the original video's natural silences, minimizing disruptive overlaps. Our analysis across frontier MLLMs reveals that while models accurately describe visual events and substantially reduce speech overlaps, gaps persist in narrative pacing and flow. Finally, we empirically validate that our automated and reference-free metrics correlate significantly with human quality ratings from sighted raters and 7 BLV participants, finding that while users narrowly prefer human-authored audio descriptions, they find MLLM-generated audio descriptions highly beneficial for comprehension. We provide actionable system design guidance and release MTG-AD at https://hf.co/datasets/google/mind-the-gap-inline-ad and MTG-AD-Eval at https://github.com/google/mtg-ad.

title: Activation Probes Are Reliable With a Handful of Positive Examples
abstract: Efforts to monitor advanced AI for rare misalignments face a data challenge: abundant aligned examples but only a handful of misaligned ones. We test activation probes in this "few vs. thousands" regime on spam and honesty detection tasks. For our tasks, training with many negative examples is on average more positive-sample-efficient than balanced training for small numbers (1-10) of positive samples. We also find that LLM upsampling can provide a performance boost equivalent to roughly doubling the number of real positive samples, though excessive upsampling hurts performance. Finally, we show a positive scaling trend, where larger models are more positive-sample-efficient to probe. Our findings suggest we should leverage the large number of negative samples available to amplify the signal from rare but critical misalignment examples.

title: DEG: Diffusion-Enhanced GFlowNet for Solving Vehicle Routing Problems
abstract: Traditional neural solvers for solving vehicle routing problems (VRPs) often suffer from limited solution diversity, motivating the development of Generative Flow Network (GFlowNet)-based models. However, the effectiveness of these models is frequently constrained by insufficient flow expansion in high-reward regions, limiting their ability to distribute probability across promising solution routes. Deeper exploration could yield superior results. Diffusion models, in contrast, provide stronger structural guidance for exploration. These two paradigms are naturally complementary: GFlowNet can supply edge-level signals for diffusion to embed, while diffusion can guide broader exploration. Leveraging this synergy, we propose Diffusion-Enhanced GFlowNet (DEG), a novel framework that integrates GFlowNet with a diffusion model to encourage richer flow expansion toward high-reward regions and derive higher-quality solutions. Specifically, DEG exploits GFlowNet's inherent diversity to generate edge-specific backward signals, applies the stochastic noise schedule of diffusion to perturb these signals, and then denoises them within the GFlowNet paradigm. To further improve scalability, we introduce a specialized decoder capable of dynamically adapting to diverse problem scales. Extensive experimental evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets, including instances with up to 10,000 nodes, demonstrate that DEG consistently achieves favorable performance compared to baseline methods.

title: What Breaks When Facts Become Stories? The Distortions Source-Agreement Metrics Miss When Models Retell Real Events
abstract: Language models are now widely used to turn recorded facts into media for public consumption, yet evaluation of such output still assumes agreement with the source as its measure of success. In reconstruction, where departing from the source can itself be the goal, this criterion measures the wrong construct: applied as is, it counts intended departures as errors; withheld, it lets real distortion through. We had three model families rewrite 2,000 news articles as summaries and as stories, measured what changed on every axis of the five Ws and how, and asked of each detected distortion whether the assigned perspective warranted it, which set a third of them aside. Time and manner were not lost but replaced, while place and causation lost the expressions that carry them. Accountability distortion behaved otherwise. Barely present in summaries, it rose up to sevenfold in stories, and of those whose direction could be determined, two in three lightened the perpetrator's responsibility. Such distortions survive claim-level fact checking and leave the retelling grammatically cleaner than its source. Where our judges disagreed, three authors relabeling the same cases converged on whether a distortion had occurred but not on whether it was warranted, a boundary contested rather than merely hard to detect. To support work on detecting and reducing them, we release ReTold-2k, a reconstructable corpus with the scoring protocol and per-judge baselines kept unaggregated.(https://github.com/Retold2K/retold2k).

title: Sparse Fine-Tuning for Parameter-Efficient Adversarial Training
abstract: Deep neural networks achieve strong performance across many tasks but remain vulnerable to adversarial perturbations. Adversarial training (AT) is one of the most effective defenses, yet it suffers from high memory cost on large models and the persistent clean-robust accuracy trade-off. Recent work introduces parameter-efficient fine-tuning, such as LoRA, into AT, but this constraint induces a notable robustness gap relative to full-parameter AT. In this work, we revisit parameter-efficient adversarial fine-tuning from a parameter space perspective. Through gradient analysis, we find that adversarial optimization is highly concentrated on a small subset of parameters, which we call Robustness-Critical Parameters (RCPs), suggesting that robustness is encoded in a sparse subspace. Building on this observation, we propose Sparse Adversarial Fine-Tuning (SAFT), which identifies RCPs via adversarial gradient saliency and performs AT by updating only these parameters while freezing the rest. Across architectures and datasets, SAFT outperforms LoRA-based methods in both clean and robust accuracy with fewer trainable parameters, and approaches or surpasses full parameter AT in robustness while updating only about 5\% of parameters.

title: End-to-End Guarantees for Masked Diffusion Models under Conditional Mixing
abstract: Masked diffusion models train a denoiser on masked cross-entropy and generate by unmasking many positions in parallel. Existing MDM sampling bounds assume an exact denoiser or leave its error uncontrolled while training bounds cover only the masking distribution on which the model was trained. We present an end-to-end guarantee for a learned denoiser under conditional mixing (CM): stationary sources (e.g. floored order-$r$ Markov and two-sided-Doeblin hidden-Markov sources) for which revealing distant visible tokens moves a masked token's posterior on average exponentially little in the distance with correlation length $τ_c$. We show the empirical risk minimizer trained under any masking distribution attains per-token excess $\varepsilon'$ on that distribution from $\varepsilon'^{-\mathcal{O}(τ_c\log|\mathcal{V}|)}$ training sequences, independent of sequence length $N$ -- one sample budget serves every decoding schedule when each schedule's denoiser is trained under its own weighting. We further show that the exponent's order $Θ(τ_c\log|\mathcal{V}|)$ is minimax-optimal up to constants; more efficient rates require added structure. With this, we bound the end-to-end KL as $\mathrm{KL}(π\Vert p_{\mathrm{alg}})\leq \varepsilon+N\varepsilon'$ under a dilated schedule of $T=\mathcal{O}(τ_c\log(N|\mathcal{V}|/\varepsilon))$ denoising steps versus $Ω(N)$ steps for a fixed random order on an explicit CM source. Finally, we show that block-autoregressive samplers chain across blocks with no added error and that a $Λ$-looped order-$r$ message-passing class on order-$r$ sources achieves polynomial sample complexity, with approximation error improving per loop until saturation at $Λr\approx τ_c\log(1/\varepsilon')$. Experiments on released and retrained models support our results' qualitative predictions.

title: Unlocking Any-Order Generation in Pretrained Autoregressive Image Models
abstract: Autoregressive (AR) image generators are powerful in principle but inflexible in practice: training with a fixed raster-scan order hardcodes a single factorization of the image distribution into the model, leaving it unable to inpaint, outpaint, or edit at inference time. Existing solutions, including the modern discrete-diffusion family, train from scratch on a mixture of token orderings, paying roughly 3x the compute of standard raster-scan training; discrete diffusion further sacrifices compatibility with the AR inference ecosystem (KV caching, vLLM) by construction. We argue that this cost is unnecessary. A pretrained raster-scan AR model has already learned the joint distribution over image tokens; what it lacks is not knowledge but the ability to express that knowledge through non-sequential conditional pathways. We propose a recipe for adapting pretrained raster-scan models into any-order generators using two components: future-aware positional embeddings that resolve a target-position identifiability problem at negligible overhead, and an ordering curriculum that traces a stable optimization path from the pretrained solution to a good any-order basin. Applied to four base models across two architectures and two scales (LlamaGen-L/XL, RAR-L/XL), the recipe substantially outperforms MaskGIT on ImageNet inpainting (FID 6.21 vs. 10.44) and outpainting, is competitive with MAR-L, trades a 1.2-1.9 increase in class-conditional FID for this flexibility, and costs 13-33% additional compute beyond pretraining, while leaving the standard AR inference stack untouched. Inpainting, outpainting, and editing, our results suggest, need not be added to autoregressive image models. They can be unlocked from the ones that exist. Code is available at https://github.com/Ordered-AR/unlockedadaptation.

title: A Novel Approach to Evaluating Evaluation Metrics for Multi-Output Structured Prediction
abstract: In multi-output structured prediction tasks, while only one ground truth label may be provided in the training data, multiple equally valid outputs may be possible, making reliable evaluation a persistent challenge. We postulate that human evaluators implicitly use task-specific invariants, e.g., object boundaries in colorized images or named entities in translations, to judge if an output is acceptable. Under this assumption, we introduce a notion of approximate task-specific invariants and use them as diagnostic tools to evaluate a variety of existing metrics for vision and language tasks. We use these task invariants as part of a framework to systematically test metric reliability by encouraging domain-relevant invariants in model outputs via an augmented loss function. In our experiments, we observe that enforcing invariants with an augmented loss yields substantial improvements in popular distributional metrics while more traditional metrics change only marginally. Through this invariants-driven evaluation, we expose where standard metrics fail to detect meaningful differences, and we highlight the conditions under which distributional metrics succeed or still fall short.

title: Uncertainty-Guided Cross-Modal Alignment for Diffusion-Based IoT Intrusion Detection
abstract: Diffusion models evolve noisy states toward a learned data distribution, so their sampling behavior depends on the geometry of the representation in which denoising occurs. This dependence is especially important for multimodal data: independently trained encoders can map synchronized views to incompatible latent regions, while uniform alignment can let an uncertain view distort the shared geometry. To address this gap, we introduce a novel reliability-guided alignment rule that uses normalized VAE posterior variance to control directional cross-modal influence before diffusion training. We study this issue in minority-attack generation for imbalanced Internet-of-Things intrusion detection. Tabular flow attributes, a DeepInsight image, and a packet sequence are encoded by modality-specific variational autoencoders. Per-modality normalized VAE posterior variances provide bounded, sample-specific weighting signals in an asymmetric stop-gradient alignment objective. We use these quantities as heuristic encoder-derived reliability proxies rather than calibrated probabilistic uncertainties. The full modality-specific latent means obtained after alignment fine-tuning are standardized and modeled jointly by a class-conditional EDM; a second-order sampler then generates paired attack-conditioned latent blocks for the three decoders. In controlled experiments on TON-IoT, uncertainty-aware alignment obtains the highest mean precision, recall, density, and coverage among three diffusion variants. Augmenting only the training split yields ROC-AUC 0.9515, PR-AUC 0.8954, balanced accuracy 0.8395, and attack-class F1 0.7940 on an untouched real test set. Among the two variants with matched alignment fine-tuning, posterior-variance-based weighting improves both tabular generative fidelity and downstream detection relative to uniform weighting.

title: PALATE: Pretrained Autoregressive LATent Embeddings
abstract: Local-commerce and food-delivery marketplaces run large ads businesses: across hundreds of thousands of stores, merchants pay to be surfaced on browse and search surfaces, and a ranker decides which ads each consumer sees. Ranking well demands strong per-consumer personalization, yet a consumer's raw interaction history is sparse and high-cardinality. Our production ranker had personalized only through hand-engineered signals: aggregate engagement counts, categorical embeddings, and order-agnostic pooled history, with no learned per-consumer sequence representation. We learn one by training a GPT-style generative model of the consumer's engagement sequence to predict their next few engagements, and read its last-token hidden state as the consumer embedding. That single frozen vector becomes one shared personalization input for every ad surface: a daily job refreshes it, and each ranker consumes it as an ordinary dense feature. Offline it is the largest single-feature gain in our ranking-AUC ladder, a relative Eval-AUC gain of +0.59% on a browse-driven feed and +0.57% on a query-driven search surface. Online, it shipped as one component of bundled ranker retrains on both surfaces: Discovery (revenue +0.79%, conversion rate +1.17%) and Search (revenue +0.94%, conversion rate +1.50%). Three design choices adapt the generative objective to a repurchase-heavy marketplace, and are the core of our contribution: an exploration-weighted loss that up-weights businesses new to the consumer over ones already engaged; a two-stage curriculum: a click pretrain that keeps the representation broad and exploratory, then a conversion fine-tune that sharpens purchase intent; and a designed negative set that pairs a fixed popular-business pool and businesses shown but not ordered with random and in-batch negatives.

title: Certified Access: Test-Time Compute on Conservative Physics-Structured AI Memory
abstract: Test-time compute mechanisms, such as retries, confidence-based escalation and non-local routing, are conventionally deployed as black-box additions to trained models. They typically add forward passes or halting heads, but give no structural account of what the extra compute buys or what it costs against the model's stability guarantees. We therefore propose a theoretical and empirical framework for test-time compute on a Latent Dynamics Model used as the memory. When an encoder's latent state $(q,p)$ is advanced by a damped symplectic (velocity-Verlet) step of a learned Hamiltonian, every mechanism that expands access has an exact phase-volume Jacobian, a bounded energy change and an exact latch-transport law. We split reachability failures into escape failures and reach failures. A Lorentz squeeze resolves escape failures by injecting bounded, re-absorbable energy. A gated canonical translation (a one-step channel across $C_T$) resolves reach failures at $\detJ=1$ exactly. We verify this certificate stack on a designed analytic testbed. Reaching just beyond $C_T$ with the squeeze requires energy that grows quadratically in the excess distance. The gated channel's energy cost equals the potential difference between its endpoints, which is zero on the matched channel measured here, and so does not grow with distance in this testbed. An untrained state-replacing map annihilates phase volume and erases stored charge, while the gated channel transports it. On a learned physics-structured memory, we show calibrated compute rationing and evaluate the scaling limits of non-local routing against a physics-free baseline. The main contribution is the formalization and verification of the certificate stack, not benchmark performance.

title: FairSplit: Decomposing the Embedding Space for Fair Classification
